The consulting and recruiting supply chains have been broken for decades. AI is simply exposing the damage, whether the functional and corporate silos involved choose to acknowledge it or not.

Job descriptions are fantasy creations for people who do not exist, written as though human beings were checklists to be filled with keywords. Critical thinking disappears. There is little meaningful distinction between three years and 33 years of experience. Recruiters distribute mass emails and texts, hoping an algorithm catches a match.

By the time meaningful dialogue occurs, the candidate, the opportunity, or both are long gone.

Hiring managers reach out to people they already know while highly capable talent remains available through other networks. Then those networks introduce Byzantine statements of work and agreements detached from operational reality. The result is remarkable: they repel the most capable people while retaining those most willing to tolerate dysfunction.

Someone who spent decades protected by one corporate and functional cocoon is not necessarily equivalent to someone who has navigated multiple corporate systems, adapted repeatedly, solved unfamiliar problems, and built an independent operating infrastructure.

Many, if not most, recruiting firms still play a numbers game: throw spaghetti at the wall and see what sticks. The good ones do something radically different. They develop long-term relationships, understand actual capability, and preserve context beyond the latest keyword search.

This is a classic configuration mismatch.

The opportunity, the requirements, the candidate, the contract, the recruiter, and the hiring manager are treated as separate documents and transactions rather than interconnected configuration items within one value stream. Information is duplicated, stripped of context, distorted at every handoff, and discovered too late.

Lean Documents and Lean Configuration can repair this broken neural system by connecting requirements, evidence, capability, decisions, constraints, and feedback at the moment they matter.

AI did not break recruiting and consulting.

It is merely making the existing failure impossible to hide.

"For the younger generation entering the workforce, ...leaning into the things AI can't replicate: curiosity, resilience and the ability to connect with people. It is rarely a shortage of talent that holds young people back, but a shortage of access to the skills that let that talent be seen..."

The AI-disruption to work is real. Entry level jobs, open to new graduates, are now being AI-rationalised as most of these tasks lend well to Digital/AI investment. Despite repeated assurances that job openings have not drastically shrunk, on the ground however, the hiring appetite is noticeably lower. And not just because AI is a magic formula. But also the economic uncertainties, the newer generational work demands etc.

Employment is no longer the target. 

As it was four decades ago when this eager graduate stepped out to find work, to stand on his own two feet, to taste, secure and enjoy independence. To be able to proudly help a single bread winner parent with the bills. There was no internet, no social media, no smart phones and watches, no laptops, and no work knowledge (no google, no AI, only library textbooks). It typically took at least a year to settle into a workplace,  and easily 2-3 years more to become reasonably good at work.  Largely subjective, based on supervisor and managers. Loyalty and likeability, including a range of affinity biases, often undergirded early potential talent assessments. 

The new graduate is still the eager job seeker. Growing up in the internet, with google as the library, social media as the tutor, and AI as the illusionary answer to work knowledge. The workplace has also drastically changed from four decades ago. Global operations, timezones, cultural differences, hybrid arrangements, offshoring, contract work etc. Most importantly,  overworked, overstretched, and under-appreciated middle managers (think Gallup's recent survey) whose tolerance for new graduate blurness, or know-it-all behaviours, will be low. The very same middle managers who would need to guide and mentor the new graduates through the work steps.

Employability is now the demand. 

"...curiosity, resilience and the ability to connect with people..."

These are work skills, quite different from academic skills and technical skills. And new graduates will do well to be able to gain these fast, and demonstrate these skills as abilities, within months of joining an organisation. Not years. And not expected the middle manager to hand hold. And not expecting to find AI solutions to work problems encountered. But learning to think WITH AI.

Reading Semicon India 2026 as a dataset, not a headline.

The event closed with Rs 1 lakh crore (~USD 11-12B) in commitments, ~1 lakh projected jobs, and 25 MoUs and announcements. As a data and business analyst, my first question is which of these are leading indicators and which are noise.

1. Funnel analysis

Semicon 1.0 approval → production: 3 of 12 units live = 25%
Design start-ups supported → VC-funded: 20 of 105 = ~19%
Semicon 2.0 design target: 200 start-ups (~1.9x the phase-one cohort)

Each stage has a different lag. Approval-to-production takes years, so the current 25% will rise as the cohort matures. Reading it as a failure rate would be a cohort-timing error.

2. Data quality flags

Commitment ≠ capex. The Rs 1 lakh crore depends on board and shareholder approvals over 2-3 years.
MoU ≠ signed supply contract. It is a soft signal with no volume or price attached.
Capital intensity check: Rs 1 lakh crore / 1 lakh jobs ≈ Rs 1 crore per job. That is a plausible fab/OSAT ratio, but it's a useful sanity test on the jobs claim.

3. Illustrative sensitivity (my assumption, not reported data)
If commitment-to-capex conversion is 50% / 70% / 90%, realised investment is roughly Rs 50k / 70k / 90k crore. The spread is the real uncertainty.

4. Where the supply chain signal is

Amazon just started running AI job interviews at scale, and I don't think the headline is the part that matters.

Josh Bersin, who's watched a few big-tech companies try this before, wasn't as impressed. "Google tried this. Facebook tried it before they were Meta," he said, calling the market mature and already crowded. A hyperscaler's name on the box doesn't automatically win a domain fight.

A GA announcement can't answer the question that actually decides this. Shipping the interview is the easy part. Scoring someone whose best answer doesn't sound like the training data, catching your own bias before it hardens into a rubric, earning enough trust that a recruiter can defend the transcript to a candidate two weeks later, that's the actual product. Compute and distribution don't shortcut any of it.

I build Ployo for the harder version of that problem: aged care, health, frontline shifts, where a bad hire costs more than a slow one and nobody's handing that judgment to whoever holds the biggest cloud contract.

Amazon showing up doesn't scare me. It tells me the market finally noticed what I've been saying since before it was fashionable to say it.

The Illusion of Flexibility: What Independent Contractors and Platforms Need to Know About Governance
Independent contracting is often framed around independence, agility, and mutual trust. Phrases like "work on your own terms," "flexible project placement," and "grow with us as a trusted partner" are frequently used to attract skilled workers into digital labor ecosystems.
However, when communication breakdowns occur, the reality behind these statements often reveals a significant imbalance in leverage.
Recently, my contract with Cloudfactory was terminated following a series of sudden offboardings and unclear allocation processes. Despite completing required training streams and seeking clarity through formal channels, the experience highlighted structural patterns that every independent contractor and platform operator should evaluate:
Key Takeaways for Independent Contractors
Vague Reallocation Policies: Platforms frequently retain absolute discretion over project streams, leaving contractors vulnerable to sudden offboarding without defined notice periods or clear metrics.
Asymmetric Communication: When resolution mechanisms rely on slow or automated internal ticket systems, contractors are effectively held in limbo, unable to transition quickly, yet restricted by platform commitments.
Training vs. Deployment Gaps: Completing multi-stream training modules does not always guarantee active allocation. Always clarify lead times and allocation guarantees before investing extensive unpaid or low-paid training hours.
Considerations for Companies Hiring AI & Data Talent
Retention Requires Transparency: High contractor churn and sudden account terminations diminish workforce trust and impact long-term data annotation quality.
Clear Offboarding Protocols: Providing explicit, performance-backed metrics prior to project removal builds a more reliable and motivated flexible workforce.
To fellow AI annotators and gig workers: read service level agreements carefully, diversify your client base early, and always insist on explicit written feedback when project statuses change.
